newsitem.title: DUBAI: Prices low, but spirits rise in Dubai gold market.
newsitem.headline: Prices low, but spirits rise in Dubai gold market.

text.p: Prices were lower, but spirits were rising in the Dubai gold market on Sunday as traders said demand was gaining strength in the second week of Ramadan, ahead of the Eid al-Fitr holidays -- a traditionally buoyant time for sales.
"The prices are good for the customers at the moment. Lower prices have boosted demand and we don't expect them to climb very much this week," said one trader.

In line with international bullion prices, which last week hit 3-1/2 year lows before recovering slightly, Dubai's benchmark ten tola bar was quoted by traders at between 4,913 dirhams ($1,339) and 4,917 dirhams, down from last week's 4,960 dirhams.
A ten tola bar is 3.746 ounces of 24 carat gold.
On the world market, gold was last traded on Saturday at $355.50/$356.00 an ounce, off the previous week's $358.70/9.20 an ounce level.
Traders in the Middle East's leading gold centre said indications pointed to brighter sales in the next few weeks of the Islamic fasting month of Ramadan.

They included expectations that international prices would not recover sharply in the short term, the ongoing wedding season in India -- the world's single largest gold market -- and the Eid al-Fitr religious festival marking the end of Ramadan.
The holiday, due to fall around February 10, customarily involves an exchange of gifts -- gold being a popular present in the oil-rich Gulf.
"We have more visitors to Dubai that are buying gold. And the lower prices are helping the market," said one trader.
"The market is moving because of the season in India. And people are beginning to buy presents for Eid," said another.
Although traders said demand from India was picking up, they said the market was sensitive to a suspension in exports from Dubai into Pakistan by the Dubai-based ARY Traders.

ARY, the sole importers of gold and silver into Pakistan, have not made any shipments in the past two weeks amid concern in Pakistan on the validity of their import licence, a company official told Reuters on Sunday.
